newsitem.title: USA: Florida faces critical sand shortage.
newsitem.headline: Florida faces critical sand shortage.

text.p: With vast stretches of beach washing into the ocean each year, Florida's $35 billion tourism industry faces a critical problem that has prompted Miami Beach to look to foreign sand to boost its shore.
Florida's beaches -- a magnet for millions of visitors and a protective buffer for billions of dollars worth of real estate -- are the bedrock of Florida's economy.
Yet more than a third of Florida's nearly 800 miles (1,280 km) of beach is classified as "critically eroding" -- a problem that some believe state legislators are ignoring.
"The state of Florida has historically taken its beaches for granted," Paden Woodruff, an environmental administrator with the state's Bureau of Beaches, said.

In November, a wicked northeast storm system underlined the issue, carving huge chunks of sand from Florida's east coast. In some areas, wind and waves ate away the beach right up to oceanfront hotel sea walls.
Along sections of world-famous Miami Beach, the storm gouged away sand up to the beach dunes, leaving five-foot (1.5-meter) bluffs draped with tangled roots of dune grasses.
"We lost about 10 feet (3 meters) of sand in the storm. Normally we lose about a foot (0.3 meters) every four months," Joseph Pinon, Miami Beach assistant city manager, said.
Florida beaches have always lost sand to the relentless ebb and flow of water on the Atlantic and Gulf coasts and the occasional direct hit from a hurricane.

Some of the sand is pushed back on shore by nature. And for decades the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has staged massive renourishment projects, dredging thousands of tons of sand from the ocean floor and pumping it back onto the beach.
But experts say Florida's offshore deposits of sand are quickly disappearing, spurring cities like Miami Beach to look elsewhere for new supplies of sand.

The city was rebuffed by the Bahamas, an archipelago of some 700 islands that has plenty of sand but competes with Florida for tourist dollars, so it turned to the Turks and Caicos, a British colony south of the Bahamas.
"They are willing to sell us the sand," Pinon said. "They have about one billion tons of sand ready for export."
But Turks sand is not an exact match for Florida's coarse coral sand, prompting concerns that nesting sea turtles might be turned off by its different colour, texture and temperature.
"Their incubation is dependent on temperature," Woodruff said. "So we have to ask, 'What are we doing to marine turtles by using this material?'"

Miami Beach, in dire need of 500,000 cubic yards (382,300 cu metre) of beach sand to repair its eroding shoreline, now is testing the Turks and Caicos sand for compatibility with the endangered sea turtles that nest on its beaches.
The quest for sand is crucial to a state whose main industry is tourism.
"The beach is the most important thing," said Dennis Paschke, 26, a tourist from Dusseldorf, Germany as he strolled Miami Beach. "I don't think we would come here without it."

Restoration experts are asking state lawmakers to boost beach spending from an average of $8.6 million to more than $30 million a year, still a tiny fraction of the $35 billion that 42 million tourists spend in Florida yearly.
"There wouldn't be any tourists if there wasn't a beach," Woodruff said.

Of Florida's 787 miles (1,260 km) of Atlantic and Gulf beaches, 273 miles (435 km) are deemed "critically eroding shoreline." But at a cost of $2 million-$3.5 million per mile the state is able to restore only a few miles each year.

In addition to tourism, the beaches provide a protective buffer from storms for billions of dollars of Florida real estate, from the towering oceanfront hotels and condominiums of Miami Beach to the costly beach homes of the Panhandle.
Without wide, stable beaches, hurricane-driven tidal surges can cause catastrophic damage.
"I think we're very vulnerable (to hurricanes)," Woodruff said. "Some areas will do well. Others won't."
